title: An ordinary Monday
hookLine: At a well, on an errand, Jesus says worship needs neither this mountain nor Jerusalem
tomorrow: what did the Buddha remember about sitting in the shade as a boy?

cards: Retreat photos are mostly mountains: a yoga deck above the clouds, a monastery on a cliff. Then the alarm goes off on Monday. John's Gospel has a story for that gap.

Jesus, tired from the road, sits down by a well. A Samaritan woman comes out to draw water, an ordinary errand on an ordinary day, and he asks her for a drink. Their talk turns to an old argument between their peoples.
Her ancestors worshiped on this mountain, she says, and his people say Jerusalem. So which mountain is it?

teach.b: Jesus answers: "Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father."
Then he says where: "the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth." Christians take this as a teaching about place: God isn't kept on one mountain.
God is met in spirit and in truth, which can happen at a well with a water jar. Here's a neighbor who says something close.
In the Chan Buddhist tradition of China, Layman Pang, a householder and not a monk, wrote that his miraculous power and wondrous activity was drawing water and carrying firewood.
What they share: the holy found in the plainest chore, even the same water.
An honest difference: Jesus speaks of worshiping the Father, a God who seeks people out; Layman Pang names no God, and the wonder is the chore itself. Neither one needs a mountain.
That's what this path carries into the ordinary days. A practice that only works on retreat isn't finished yet. Monday is where it's tested: your rule, done plainly, on a day when nothing happens.

how: Christians read Jesus' words at the well as worship not bound to one holy place; Chan Buddhists point to Layman Pang's water and firewood. People on this path keep their rule on plain days, not only on retreat.

o: the first day back after a long holiday away
a plain workday where your practice still counts
a day off set aside only for a spiritual retreat

games.q: the well and the firewood: tap the pairs.
p: where worship happens, not a mountain

s: in John's Gospel, Jesus meets the woman on an ordinary errand at a well
she came to draw water; he was tired from the road and asked her for a drink.
at the well, Jesus tells her Jerusalem is the one right place to worship
he says the hour comes when worship is neither on this mountain nor at Jerusalem.
spiritual practice needs a special place to really work
the popular idea. at the well it's spirit and truth; for Layman Pang, water and firewood.

games.q: a friend says she can only meditate on her yearly retreat; at home it 'doesn't count.' what fits the well and Layman Pang?
o: it counts at home: neither this mountain nor that, and even drawing water is practice.
she's right: some places are holy, so save the real practice for those.
skip the retreat: real practice means never leaving home at all.
games.why: Jesus told the woman at the well that worship isn't bound to this mountain or Jerusalem; Layman Pang found wonder in water and firewood. a plain day is place enough.

practice: Listen to one ordinary sound around you: a fridge humming, traffic, a door down the hall. For the rest of the sit, let that plain sound be the place, and each time your mind goes looking for somewhere better, come back to it.

wordCard.voice: An ordinary Monday: a plain day, which, in the story at the well, is place enough. Worship needs no mountain.

orig.note: Greek, John 4:23: in spirit and in truth.

carryVoice: The line to keep: plain days, a well and a water jar, no mountain. Day one of fourteen ordinary ones.

sources.ref: John 4:6-9 and 4:20 (Jesus tired at the well; the Samaritan woman comes to draw water; 'our fathers worshipped in this mountain')
